questions.q: A 35-year-old farmer presents with a painless ulcer on his right hand with rolled, indurated edges and satellite lymphadenopathy. He reports working with soil and plants. A smear from the lesion shows gram-positive branching filaments. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Actinomycosis presents with painless indurated lesions, sinus tracts, and sulfur granules. The gram-positive branching filaments are characteristic of Actinomyces israelii. The clinical context of soil exposure supports this. Nocardia also shows branching filaments but is weakly acid-fast and typically affects immunocompromised patients.

questions.q: A 28-year-old immunocompetent patient presents with confluent hypopigmented scaly patches on the upper trunk. KOH preparation shows 'spaghetti and meatballs' pattern. Which organism is responsible and what is the first-line topical treatment?
questions.exp: Pityriasis versicolor is caused by Malassezia furfur (now classified as M. globosa/restricta). KOH shows short hyphae and round yeast cells resembling 'spaghetti and meatballs'. First-line topical treatment is selenium sulfide 2.5% or ketoconazole shampoo. Fluconazole is used for systemic treatment.

questions.q: A 22-year-old sexually active male presents with painful grouped vesicles on an erythematous base on the glans penis. Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells. He had a similar episode 6 months ago. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Acyclovir 400 mg TID for 5 days as episodic therapy
Acyclovir 400 mg BID daily as suppressive therapy
questions.exp: Recurrent genital herpes (>6 episodes/year) warrants daily suppressive therapy. Acyclovir 400mg BID or valacyclovir 500mg OD are standard suppressive regimens. Suppressive therapy reduces recurrence frequency by 70-80% and reduces viral shedding, decreasing transmission risk.

questions.q: A 45-year-old male presents with a painless, indurated ulcer on his penis for 3 weeks. There is non-tender inguinal lymphadenopathy. VDRL test is non-reactive. What is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?
opts: Dark field microscopy of ulcer exudate
questions.exp: Primary syphilis (chancre) can be VDRL-negative in early stages. Dark field microscopy of exudate from the ulcer is the gold standard for diagnosing primary syphilis by directly visualizing T. pallidum. TPHA/FTA-ABS are useful but may also be negative in very early primary syphilis.

questions.q: A 30-year-old male from rural India presents with thickened, painless hypopigmented patches on his cheek and arm. Examination reveals loss of sensation to light touch in the patches. Slit skin smear shows 1+ AFB. What type of leprosy does he have according to Ridley-Jopling classification?
questions.exp: Borderline tuberculoid (BT) leprosy presents with multiple (2-5) hypopigmented patches with partial sensory loss. Bacillary index of 1+ is seen in BT. TT has single lesion with complete sensory loss and negative smear. BT is more common and unstable, prone to reactions.

questions.q: A 40-year-old female presents with butterfly rash on the face, photosensitivity, and oral ulcers for 3 months. ANA titer is 1:640 with anti-dsDNA antibody positive. Which complement pathway is primarily activated in SLE skin lesions?
questions.exp: In SLE, immune complex deposition (IgG/IgM + complement) in skin triggers the classical complement pathway via C1q binding to immune complexes. This leads to C3 consumption and local tissue damage. The lupus band test shows IgG, IgM, and C3 deposits at the dermoepidermal junction.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male presents with tense bullae on normal-appearing and erythematous skin, predominantly on the trunk and flexures. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 deposits along the basement membrane zone. What is the target antigen?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid targets BP180 (BPAG2) and BP230. BP180 is a transmembrane protein in hemidesmosomes at the basement membrane. Antibodies against BP180 NC16A domain are most pathogenic. DIF shows linear IgG+C3 along BMZ. Desmoglein 3 is the target in pemphigus vulgaris.

questions.q: A 65-year-old male smoker presents with a pearly white nodule with telangiectasia on his nose. Biopsy shows palisading basaloid cells with peripheral clefting and mucinous stroma. What is the most common site for metastasis if this tumor spreads?
questions.exp: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) very rarely metastasizes (<0.1%). When metastasis occurs, it goes to regional lymph nodes first, followed by lungs, bone, and skin. The histological description (palisading basaloid cells with peripheral clefting) is characteristic of nodular BCC.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with a slowly growing violaceous plaque on her lower leg following chronic lymphedema post-mastectomy. Histology shows irregular vascular channels lined by atypical endothelial cells. What is this condition called?
questions.exp: Stewart-Treves syndrome is a rare lymphangiosarcoma arising in chronic lymphedema, classically post-mastectomy. It presents as violaceous/reddish plaques or nodules. The prognosis is poor. It is distinct from Kaposi sarcoma (HHV-8 associated) and primary cutaneous angiosarcoma.

questions.q: During a punch biopsy of a lesion on the dorsum of the hand, which anatomical landmark must be identified to avoid injury to the extensor tendons?
opts: Ensure biopsy depth does not exceed 3mm
Palpate for underlying tendon before insertion
Biopsy only at the ulnar side
questions.exp: On the dorsum of the hand, extensor tendons lie superficially beneath thin dermis and subcutaneous tissue. Palpating the tendon before punch biopsy is critical. The subcutaneous tissue is minimal here, and the punch should not be advanced beyond the dermis. Angling the punch away from tendons reduces risk.

questions.q: A patient on long-term methotrexate for psoriasis develops megaloblastic anemia. What supplementation should have been given to prevent this, and at what timing relative to methotrexate?
opts: Folic acid 5mg daily, taken on the same day as methotrexate
Folic acid 5mg weekly, taken 24-48 hours after methotrexate dose
Folinic acid 15mg, taken 6 hours before methotrexate
questions.exp: Folic acid supplementation (1-5mg/day or 5mg weekly) should be given the day after methotrexate, not on the same day, to reduce side effects (nausea, mucositis, megaloblastic anemia) without significantly reducing efficacy. Folinic acid (leucovorin) is used for rescue in toxicity, not routine supplementation.

questions.q: A 32-year-old female with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis fails topical therapy. She is started on acitretin. What is the mandatory contraception advice?
opts: Contraception for 1 month after stopping acitretin
Contraception for 2 years after stopping acitretin
Contraception for 3 years after stopping acitretin
Contraception only during therapy, no need after stopping
questions.exp: Acitretin is converted to etretinate (especially with alcohol consumption), which has an elimination half-life of 80-175 days and can be detected for up to 3 years. Women of childbearing potential must use effective contraception during treatment and for 3 years after stopping acitretin due to potent teratogenicity.

questions.q: A 25-year-old male presents with recurrent episodes of target lesions on the dorsum of hands, following a herpes labialis episode. The current episode is the 4th in a year. What is the most appropriate preventive treatment?
opts: Topical acyclovir cream applied early in each episode
questions.exp: Herpes-associated erythema multiforme (HAEM) is the most common trigger (>50% cases). For frequent recurrences (>5/year), daily suppressive antiviral therapy with acyclovir 400mg BID or valacyclovir 500mg OD for 6 months prevents HSV reactivation and subsequent EM episodes. Steroids may worsen HSV.

questions.q: A 60-year-old diabetic male presents with painful, deep-seated fluctuant nodule in the nasolabial fold that has been enlarging for 2 weeks. Gram stain of pus shows gram-positive cocci in clusters. What is the most dangerous complication of this condition?
questions.exp: Furuncle/carbuncle in the 'danger triangle' of the face (nasolabial fold to upper lip) drains via angular vein to ophthalmic veins and cavernous sinus. Squeezing or improper drainage can lead to cavernous sinus thrombosis, which is life-threatening. This is why nasolabial furuncles should not be squeezed.

questions.q: A 35-year-old HIV-positive patient (CD4 count 150 cells/μL) presents with extensive verrucous plaques on the hands and feet. Biopsy shows koilocytosis and HPV-associated changes. Which HPV types are most commonly responsible for deep palmoplantar warts?
questions.exp: Myrmecia (deep palmoplantar warts) are caused by HPV type 1, while mosaic warts on palms/soles are caused by HPV type 2. HPV 6/11 cause condyloma acuminata (anogenital warts). HPV 16/18 are high-risk oncogenic types causing cervical carcinoma and Bowen's disease. HPV 3/10 cause plane warts.

questions.q: A 50-year-old male presents with a non-healing ulcer on his scrotum with irregular margins. He is a chimney sweep. Biopsy confirms squamous cell carcinoma. Which carcinogen is classically associated with his occupation?
questions.exp: Scrotal carcinoma in chimney sweeps (Pott's carcinoma, 1775) was the first described occupational cancer, caused by polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) in soot. PAHs require metabolic activation to reactive epoxides that bind DNA. Arsenic causes Bowen's disease and keratoses (arsenical keratosis).

questions.q: A 28-year-old pregnant woman (32 weeks) presents with intensely pruritic papules and plaques around the umbilicus, sparing the umbilicus itself. There are tense bullae. DIF shows linear C3 and IgG along BMZ. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.exp: Pemphigoid gestationis (herpes gestationis) presents in late pregnancy with periumbilical papules/plaques (sparing umbilicus), bullae, and intense pruritus. DIF shows linear C3/IgG at BMZ. Treatment is oral prednisolone 0.5mg/kg/day. It poses fetal risk (prematurity, small for gestational age). Dapsone is contraindicated in pregnancy.

questions.q: A 20-year-old male presents with recurrent oral ulcers (>3 episodes/year), pseudofolliculitis, and uveitis. Pathergy test is positive. What HLA type is strongly associated with this condition?
questions.exp: Behçet's disease is characterized by recurrent oral ulcers, genital ulcers, uveitis, and skin lesions (pseudofolliculitis, erythema nodosum). HLA-B51 is strongly associated, particularly in patients from the Silk Road regions. Pathergy test (positive papule/pustule at venipuncture site) is a hallmark in these patients.

questions.q: A 45-year-old female with diffuse systemic sclerosis develops digital ulcers and Raynaud's phenomenon. Her nailfold capillaroscopy shows 'giant capillaries.' Which antibody is most specific for diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis?
questions.exp: Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) antibodies are most specific for diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis (dcSSc) and are associated with ILD, digital ulcers, and worse prognosis. Anti-centromere antibodies are associated with limited cutaneous SSc (CREST syndrome). Anti-RNA pol III is associated with renal crisis and dcSSc.

questions.q: A 3-year-old child presents with honey-colored crusted lesions around the nose and mouth. Gram stain shows gram-positive cocci in chains. Cultures grow the same organism. What complication must be monitored for in this child over the next 3-6 weeks?
questions.exp: Impetigo caused by nephritogenic strains of Group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes) can lead to post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) in 2-5% of cases, 3-6 weeks after skin infection. Unlike pharyngeal infection, skin streptococcal infection does NOT cause rheumatic fever. Urinalysis monitoring is required.

questions.q: A 40-year-old male presents with well-defined erythematous plaques with silvery scales on elbows, knees, and scalp. PASI score is 18. He has failed topical steroids and phototherapy. Which biological agent targeting IL-17A is approved for moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis?
questions.exp: Secukinumab (anti-IL-17A) is a first-line biologic for moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis. Ixekizumab also targets IL-17A. Adalimumab targets TNF-α. Ustekinumab targets IL-12/23 (p40 subunit). Guselkumab targets IL-23 (p19 subunit). IL-17A inhibitors are most effective, achieving PASI 90 in ~70% of patients.

questions.q: A 6-year-old atopic child develops weeping, crusted lesions on the face after starting a new pet. Skin swabs grow Staphylococcus aureus producing exfoliative toxin. What mechanism does this toxin use to cause skin damage?
opts: Cleaves desmoglein 1 in the stratum granulosum
Binds to Toll-like receptor 2 on keratinocytes
questions.exp: Staphylococcal exfoliative toxins (ETA, ETB) act as serine proteases that specifically cleave desmoglein 1 (Dsg1) in the stratum granulosum, causing intraepidermal cleavage without inflammation. This leads to SSSS (Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome) or bullous impetigo. Dsg1 is also the target antigen in pemphigus foliaceus.

questions.q: A patient undergoing PUVA therapy for psoriasis reports blurred vision and eye discomfort. What ocular complication must be screened for, and what protective measure should have been taken?
opts: Retinal detachment; wrap-around sunglasses for 24 hours after ingestion
Cataracts (anterior subcapsular); UV-blocking wrap-around sunglasses for 12-24 hours post-ingestion
Glaucoma; dark goggles during UV session only
questions.exp: PUVA (psoralen + UVA) causes anterior subcapsular cataract due to psoralen absorption in the lens. Patients must wear UV-blocking wrap-around eyewear from the time of psoralen ingestion until sunset on treatment days (12-24 hours). Annual ophthalmological screening is mandatory. Retinal damage is not typically a concern as psoralen does not accumulate in the retina.

questions.q: A 25-year-old female with pemphigus vulgaris is started on dapsone. Prior to initiating therapy, which laboratory investigation is mandatory?
questions.exp: G6PD deficiency must be screened before starting dapsone. Dapsone causes oxidative hemolysis, and G6PD-deficient patients are at high risk for severe hemolytic anemia. Methemoglobinemia is another major side effect. While CBC is also useful, G6PD testing is the mandatory screening test before dapsone therapy.

questions.q: A 32-year-old male presents with multiple depigmented macules on the trunk and face since age 15 years. Wood's lamp examination shows chalk-white fluorescence. Examination shows absent melanocytes on biopsy. What is the pathomechanism?
opts: Failure of melanoblast migration from neural crest
questions.exp: Vitiligo is an acquired condition caused by autoimmune destruction of melanocytes. T-cell-mediated cytotoxicity (CD8+ T cells), autoantibodies against melanocyte antigens (e.g., MCHR1, gp100), and innate immune activation (IFN-γ/CXCL10 pathway) are involved. Biopsy shows absent melanocytes. Wood's lamp shows bright white fluorescence due to complete loss of melanin.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male presents with a well-defined hyperpigmented patch on the cheek (malar region) that worsens in summer. His wife has a similar lesion. Wood's lamp examination makes the pigmentation more apparent. What layer of skin contains the excess melanin?
questions.exp: Melasma shows excess melanin in the epidermis (epidermal type), dermis (dermal type), or both (mixed type). Epidermal melasma appears enhanced under Wood's lamp examination (the contrast is accentuated), while dermal melasma does not show enhancement. The epidermal type has better response to treatment. Wood's lamp enhancement indicates epidermal pigmentation.

questions.q: A 19-year-old male presents with erythematous, scaly plaques on the face, chest, and scalp. Scales are yellowish and greasy, predominantly in sebaceous areas. What is the primary pathogen implicated in this condition?
questions.exp: Seborrheic dermatitis (seborrhoeic eczema) is associated with Malassezia yeast (M. globosa, M. restricta). These lipophilic yeasts metabolize sebum triglycerides, releasing oleic acid, which disrupts the skin barrier and triggers inflammation. Treatment includes antifungal shampoos (ketoconazole, selenium sulfide) and topical steroids.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with a 3-month history of a non-healing violaceous nodule on the lower leg. She is HIV-positive with CD4 count of 80. Biopsy shows proliferating spindle cells with slit-like vascular spaces and extravasated red blood cells. What is the causative agent?
questions.exp: Kaposi sarcoma is caused by HHV-8 (KSHV - Kaposi Sarcoma Herpesvirus). In HIV-positive patients with low CD4 counts (<200), KS presents with violaceous nodules/patches, typically on legs, oral mucosa, and viscera. Histology shows spindle cells, slit-like vascular spaces, and hemosiderin deposits. Treatment includes antiretrovirals and chemotherapy.

questions.q: A 70-year-old male presents with severe burning pain in a dermatomal distribution followed by grouped vesicles on an erythematous base on the right side of the trunk. What is the antiviral of choice for this condition, and when should it be started for maximum benefit?
opts: Acyclovir 800mg 5 times daily; within 72 hours of rash onset
Valacyclovir 1g TID; within 48 hours of rash onset
Famciclovir 500mg TID; any time during the acute phase
questions.exp: Herpes zoster treatment: Acyclovir 800mg 5 times daily for 7 days, valacyclovir 1g TID for 7 days, or famciclovir 500mg TID for 7 days. Treatment should be started within 72 hours of rash onset for maximum benefit (reduces duration, severity, and post-herpetic neuralgia risk). Valacyclovir and famciclovir have better bioavailability and simpler dosing.

questions.q: A 38-year-old leprosy patient develops sudden onset of painful, tender, erythematous nodules on the face and extremities with high fever and neutrophilia. Biopsy shows dense neutrophilic infiltration with foamy macrophages. What is this reaction, and what is the treatment of choice?
opts: Type 1 lepra reaction (reversal reaction); oral prednisolone
questions.exp: Erythema Nodosum Leprosum (ENL) is a Type 2 lepra reaction occurring in lepromatous (LL) and borderline lepromatous (BL) leprosy. It is an immune complex-mediated reaction presenting with tender erythematous nodules, fever, and systemic features. Thalidomide is the treatment of choice for ENL (anti-TNF-α mechanism). Prednisolone is used in Type 1 (reversal) reactions.
